name: Research and Sources
title: Research and Sources
answer: Students need to be able to judge whether a source is trustworthy, and AI tools make that skill more urgent because chatbots can produce confident summaries containing invented quotes, wrong dates, or citations to articles that do not exist. The practical response is to teach source checking and citation directly, using library databases as the reference point, and to ask students to state how they used AI on major work. This matters because a fluent answer is not the same as a true one, and schools that build research tasks with their librarian make AI shortcuts much harder to take.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: The idea is that source evaluation becomes a taught skill rather than an assumed one, because AI chat tools can generate summaries that read smoothly while containing fabricated quotes, incorrect dates, or references to articles that do not exist. A lesson can therefore ask students to verify every claim in an AI summary against a real source, such as a library database, so they discover for themselves that fluency and accuracy are separate things. Citation practice belongs in the same unit, since students need to learn how to cite a source properly and how to record when and how they used an AI tool. Many schools now ask for a short statement of AI use attached to major assignments, which, read alongside the AI use level set for the assignment, gives teachers a clear picture of how the work was made. The problem this solves is that teachers otherwise cannot tell whether a polished piece of work reflects genuine research or an unchallenged machine summary.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom the work takes the form of a verification exercise: students take an AI generated summary and check each claim against a real source, typically a library database, and record what holds up and what does not. Citation practice runs alongside it, with students learning to cite sources properly and to describe when and how they used an AI tool. Schools commonly ask for a short statement of AI use with major assignments, which teachers read together with the AI use level assigned to that task. The text does not set out separate approaches by grade band, so the method is presented as applying across the kindergarten through twelfth grade range, with the librarian involved in designing the research unit. A research unit built with the librarian is described as one of the best defenses against AI shortcuts, because the tasks are shaped so that an AI tool cannot simply complete them.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text supplies no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. What it offers instead is the observed behaviour of the tools themselves, namely that chatbots can produce confident summaries with made up quotes, incorrect dates, or citations to articles that do not exist. The claim that students quickly learn a fluent answer is not the same as a true one is presented as a classroom outcome of the checking exercise, not as a measured finding. The further claims, that library databases offer sources that have been checked and can be cited while AI chat tools cannot promise this, and that a librarian built research unit is one of the best defenses against AI shortcuts, are stated as professional judgement. Readers should treat the whole idea as grounded in practice and in the known failure modes of chat tools rather than in published research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits begin with the tools: an AI summary may contain invented quotes, wrong dates, or citations to articles that do not exist, so nothing it produces should be treated as verified on its own. Verification has to run against a real source such as a library database, and the judgement about whether a source is good enough to rely on stays with a person, which is why librarians are described as well placed to teach source evaluation. The record keeping also depends on human decisions, since the teacher sets the AI use level for an assignment and reads the student's statement of AI use alongside it to understand how the work was made. The text does not remove teacher or librarian responsibility at any point, and it does not suggest that AI can be trusted to check itself. Nothing here is legal advice, and the arrangements described are matters of school and classroom practice.
